title: Ways to Make Change
statement:
A shop has an unlimited supply of coins of each value in `coins` (all values are different). Count the **different sets of coins** that add up to exactly `amount`.

Order does not matter: `1 + 2` and `2 + 1` are the same set. There is exactly one way to make `0` (take no coins). The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

examples.explanation: Coins of 2 can never add up to an odd amount.

hints.nudge: Count sets, not orders. What if you decide about one coin value at a time: how many of it to use?
hints.pattern: Unbounded knapsack counting: ways[a] = number of ways to make a using the coin values handled so far.
hints.walkthrough: Counting sequences of coins would count 1+2 and 2+1 twice. To count sets, process the coin values one after another and never go back: ways[a] after handling the first few coins is the number of ways to make a using only those coins. Adding a coin c means: every way to make a - c (using the coins so far, including c itself) becomes a way to make a by adding one more c. So loop the amounts upward from c and do ways[a] += ways[a - c]. The OUTER loop must be over the coins and the INNER loop over the amounts; swapping them counts orders instead of sets. O(len(coins) * amount) time, O(amount) memory. Use a 64-bit type for the table in Java and C++.
